title: Exploring sex differences in global cancer incidence and mortality and the role of national development level

sections.title: 研究问题
sections.text:
《Exploring sex differences in global cancer incidence and mortality and the role of national development level》：研究问题的原文依据。

【Introduction · p0035】Sex refers to biological characteristics, whereas sex-related differences in cancer outcomes are also shaped by gender-related factors such as societal roles, health behaviours, and health care access.3,4 While differences in cancer incidence and mortality exist between men and women,1 they are often overlooked in public health and clinical practice. Male and female differences (often referred to as sex disparities) can partly be attributed to biological factors such as variations in immune system function, hormonal profiles, molecular characteristics, and body composition.5, 6, 7, 8 The role of sex goes, however, beyond biological factors, being also shaped by cultural norms and societal roles, influencing health outcomes in other ways.9 Understanding and mapping sex differences in disease incidence and mortality are crucial, as sex affects participation in early detection programs, symptom recognition, health care-seeking behaviour, and treatment decisions10 and can point to potential targets for interventions aimed at reducing these disparities.

【Introduction · p0045】The aim of our study is threefold: firstly, we will investigate cancer incidence and mortality rates by sex worldwide using population-level data. Secondly, we will investigate global sex differences in these rates. Finally, we will examine the relationship between HDI and sex differences in cancer incidence and mortality rates. Through this comprehensive analysis, our goal was to identify insights to support targeted interventions to reduce sex differences in cancer burden globally.

sections.title: 研究方法
sections.text:
《Exploring sex differences in global cancer incidence and mortality and the role of national development level》：方法与研究设计的原文依据。

【Materials and methods · abstract-2-1】Cancer incidence and mortality data (2012-2017) were obtained from the International Agency for Research on Cancer, covering 43 countries for incidence and 60 for mortality. Only nonsex-specific cancers were included and categorised into 12 groups. Age-standardised incidence rates (ASIR) and age-standardised mortality rates (ASMRs) were calculated, with sex differences analysed using men-to-women ratios (MWRs). Linear regression was used to assess the association between Human Development Index (HDI) and MWRs across cancer types.

sections.title: 主要结果
sections.text:
《Exploring sex differences in global cancer incidence and mortality and the role of national development level》：结果的原文依据；数值与适用人群以引文为准。

【Conclusions · p0130】Our findings indicate global sex differences in cancer incidence and mortality, with men generally exhibiting higher rates for most cancers, particularly oesophageal, head and neck, and lung cancers, while thyroid cancer remains more common in women. These disparities vary considerably across countries and are especially pronounced for tobacco-related cancers. Although no significant associations were found between HDI and incidence MWRs, our findings indicate that national development influences sex differences in cancer mortality for specific cancer types, such as CNS, thyroid, and lung cancer, suggesting that the impact of HDI on sex differences is not uniform but varies by cancer site. Our findings underscore the multifactorial nature of these disparities, shaped by biological, behavioural, and sociocultural factors. The observed high MWRs for tobacco-related cancers, particularly in men, underline the need for sex-specific prevention strategies such as targeted tobacco control. Similarly, the high incidence of thyroid cancer in women, likely partly driven by overdiagnosis, points to the importance of refining diagnostic guidelines. The variation in mortality disparities by HDI suggests that health system development and access play a role in shaping sex gaps in cancer outcomes. Targeted prevention strategies, equitable access to health care, and sex-sensitive cancer control policies could help to reduce these inequalities globally.

【Results · abstract-3-1】Among the cancer types included in this study, cancers of the colorectum, stomach, and lungs showed the highest incidence and mortality. Men are 12-13 times more likely to be diagnosed with oesophageal cancer (MWR ≈ 13), over nine times more likely to die from head and neck cancers, and >6 times more likely to die from lung cancer. Thyroid cancer incidence is up to five times higher in women than in men. No clear link was found between HDI and MWRs in incidence, but HDI relates to mortality and MWRs for several cancer types, with brain and thyroid cancers showing higher male mortality, while lung cancer showing relatively higher female mortality in high-HDI countries.
